World.title: Fizz takes three in Mumbai rout
World.content:
Pace sensation Mustafizur Rahman recorded his best bowling figures of the Indian Premier League today when he finished with 3 for 16 in Sunrisers Hyderabad’s 85-run victory over Mumbai Indians at Vishakhapatnam.

The three-wicket haul took the left-armer to joint-second in the wicket-takers’ list with a total tally of 13 scalps from nine matches. He is one short of Mitchell McClenaghan, who has taken 14 wickets in 10 matches.

The 20-year-old currently has the best bowling average, 15.61, and best economy rate, 6.15, amongs bowlers who have played at least eight matches in the tournament.

The Sunrisers Hyderabad might have depended on Mustafizur a number of times in the ongoing Indian Premier League, but today was a collective effort. Ashish Nehra, Bhuvaneshwar Kumar and Barinder Sran had reduced the Mumbai Indians to 49 for 6 in nine overs before Mustafizur was given the ball.

The wily left-armer sent back Hardik Pandya with his first ball with a cutter which Pandya failed to adjust himself against. Pandya attempted a slice through point, but the ball curled away to the hands of the keeper, with the umpire judging that out even though the television replays were inconclusive.

Then in the very first ball of his second over again, Fizz bowled yet another slower delivery which moved away from the batsman, getting the edge of Tim Southee on the way to the keeper.

The man from Satkhira returned got the scalp of McClenaghan in the final delivery of his third over, getting the batsman to offer a loopy catch to midwicket.

Mustafizur did not get to bowl a fourth over as David Warner gave the other bowlers their chance to mop up the tail. And they did efficiently, bundling out the hosts for just 92 runs in 16.3 overs.

Earlier, brilliant performances from Hyderabad openers, Warner and Shikhar Dhawan helped the team post 177. Dhawan scored 82 off 57 while Warner smacked 48 off 33. Yuvraj Singh also had a good time with the bat, scoring 39 off 23.

World.title: 'Fear and hope' of foster care journey inspires teen artist
World.content:
For 16-year-old Keira Graham, putting colour to canvas has become an outlet for healing and a way to find her voice.

Originally from Ti-Tree, around two hours' drive north of Alice Springs, the Anmatjere and Arrernte teen found her permanent foster family at four years old.

"I didn't speak much in Alice Springs … I didn't speak much English. When I was a baby, I spoke Warlpiri, which is my native language," she said.

"I didn't really understand what was happening.

"I remember they welcomed me … that's what made me feel like maybe this could be home."

Keira Graham says her family and Indigenous culture inspire her storytelling. (ABC News: Marina Trajkovich)

It was Keira's case worker who first gifted her art supplies, inspiring her creative talents while the family lived in an underground home in Coober Pedy.

Keira represents her experience coming into care through her self-portraits. (ABC News: Marina Trajkovich)

Keira said her journey as an artist and her self-portraits have helped her process her experiences in foster care.

"The one of myself is my journey of coming into care," she said.

"The background is full of movement and colour. It's my way of showing everything I carry, the fear, the silence, the hope, and love I eventually found. This painting holds all of that."

Keira says this piece shows her relationship with her grandma, with her family often represented in her work. (ABC News: Marina Trajkovich)

"It does help me express myself … through colour or animals, or stories.

"One is about my brother and me. We like to go to the beach a lot, and we like to find crabs."

Hobby turned career

Keira says her art has been a key part of processing and sharing her journey. (ABC News: Marina Trajkovich)

Now living with her family in Port Macquarie on the New South Wales Mid North Coast, Keira's artwork has quickly gone from hobby to a promising career.

The Northern Territory Department of Children and Families has purchased one of Keira's self-portraits for their Alice Springs office to inspire other children in foster care.

Mparntwe country and the red sand of Alice Springs also feature in a netball uniform Keira designed through an art competition with the Alice Springs Netball Association.

Keira entered and won a competition hosted by the Alice Springs Netball Association to design new uniforms. (ABC News: Marina Trajkovich)

After debuting at the NT Link competition in Darwin last June, her designs can now be seen on courts across the territory.

"A family friend told me about the competition," Keira said.

" I didn't really expect to win, but I did. I was really proud to see my design on the dresses and the players. "

While living in Muswellbrook, in the NSW Upper Hunter region, the Wanaruah Local Aboriginal Land Council and a local energy company reached out to Keira to create artwork for a community engagement campaign.

Keira, who loves playing basketball and netball, says she was proud to see her designs being worn on the court. (Supplied: Celina Whan Creative Photography)

In December, her work attracted the attention of a former Olympian.

"I wasn't expecting that Keira was only going to be 16," Olympic sprinter turned bobsledder Jana Pittman said.

Jana Pittman discovered Keira's work online and says she's proud to be a new buyer. (ABC News: Marina Trajkovich)

The two-time World Champion and four-time Commonwealth Champion said she began collecting Aboriginal art after competing with fellow Olympic legend Cathy Freeman to help her children learn about Indigenous history and culture.

Now an obstetrician in Port Macquarie, Pittman found Keira's work while scrolling online.

"I found this beautiful piece of art that took my imagination straight away," she said.

" I'm a women's health doctor, and that painting I've also found out relates to women and passing down heritage and birthing, things like that. "

Keira said the piece was a tribute to women, particularly those who have helped shape her life.

Jana Pittman says she was particularly inspired by the piece about empowering women. (ABC News: Marina Trajkovich)

"I didn't actually expect someone like [Jana] to be buying my paintings," she said.

"It's about women and empowering women … it's for grandmothers, mothers, sisters, aunties," she said.

"The circles represent the creation of life … it's a mix of modern art and traditional dot painting too."

Keira describes her work as a mix of traditional and modern art and says it helps her connect with her Indigenous culture. (ABC News: Marina Trajkovich)

Keira's parents, Tiffany and Ben Swan, said art had helped their daughter come out of her shell.

"I do feel that she is expressing herself through her artwork," Ms Swan said.

"She's just blown us away with how well she's doing."

Stories about Keira's family, colours, or animals often feature in her paintings. (ABC News: Marina Trajkovich)

"It's been wonderful as a parent to see her grow and gain confidence," Mr Swan said.

"She has a bright future, I think."

World.title: Anzac biscuit-tin guitars sold to aid veteran charity
World.content:
If you're looking for Adrian "Ace" Kitson, you'll likely find him in his garage, hunched over a dimly lit workbench, deep in concentration.

A tuning peg in hand, he gently adjusts the strings of his latest creation until it sounds just right.

The Tasmanian musician-turned-guitar-maker has spent the better part of two years handcrafting a collection of cigar-box guitars made from Anzac biscuit tins and local timber.

The guitars are made from biscuit tins by Tasmanian bakery Cripps. (ABC News: Georgia Hogge)

On one, a rifle cartridge functions as a whammy bar. On another, a gun belt is fastened in place of a guitar strap.

Once complete, Mr Kitson intends to sell the guitars and donate the proceeds to Open Arms, a mental health charity that offers military-focused counselling services for veterans.

It is a project close to his heart.

"I've had friends who have served in the armed forces [as well as] family, my grandfather," he said.

" I feel very sorry for a lot of veterans who returned from overseas who suffer terribly from all sorts of mental illnesses. "

The guitars are short — like a banjo — and have fewer strings than a typical guitar. (ABC News: Georgia Hogge)

Mr Kitson knows firsthand the importance of veteran charities such as Open Arms.

Thirty years earlier, an incident on a night out left Mr Kitson with a traumatic brain injury. He says he has had post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) ever since.

Mr Kitson said he was not able to access support when he needed it.

"It kind of spurs me to do what I can to try to help," he said.

Homemade guitars playable

As well as being novel, each of Mr Kitson's creations is a functional instrument, although with a shorter neck and fewer strings than a standard guitar.

When played acoustically, the guitars produce a banjo-like sound due to the tin body.

A retrofitted piezo pick-up means it can be connected to an amplifier.

"You've got to be able to play them," he said.

" What's the point of having them if you can't grab it off the wall and say, 'look what I can do'? "

Despite their unconventional design and short scale, all of the instruments are playable. (ABC News: Georgia Hogge)

While Mr Kitson's goal is ultimately to raise money, he also hopes the guitars can bring joy to those who buy them.

"When you pass them on to someone else and you see the joy in their face when they get it, that's just priceless," he said.

"I love making people happy."

Guitar inspired by VC hero Teddy Sheean

There is one particularly special guitar that will not be for sale.

Honouring local war hero, Edward 'Teddy' Sheean VC, the guitar will be donated to the Latrobe RSL sub-branch to be kept on display.

Sheean, who was born in Lower Barrington in Tasmania's north-west and spent his childhood in Latrobe, held the rank of ordinary sailor in the Royal Australian Navy during World War II.

A statue of Edward 'Teddy' Sheean VC has been erected in Latrobe. (ABC News: Mackenzie Heard)

He was 18 when he died defending his ship from Japanese fire in 1942.

In 2020, he was posthumously awarded a Victoria Cross after a long-running campaign by surviving family members.

"He means a lot to the local area," Jason Bloom, secretary of the Latrobe RSL sub-branch, said.

"We have erected a statue in his honour … the RSL has various mementos of him."

Latrobe RSL secretary Jason Bloom. (ABC News: Mackenzie Heard)

In the four years he has been in his role as secretary, Mr Kitson's guitar is the first physical donation he's received.

"They are awesome. He's done a superb job on them guitars," Mr Bloom said.

"There's a lot of time put into them and hopefully we can sell a few for him."

World.title: Surfer turns decommissioned wind turbine blades into surfboard fins
World.content:
At the Waubra Wind Farm near Ballarat, 40-metre turbine blades that once helped power the state are being sent away for a second life.

Far from the frigid, windswept fields of western Victoria, small parts of the fibreglass turbine blades are carving through waves along the New South Wales northern beaches.

Sydney surfer Banjo Hunt has been repurposing a 6m section of a blade from the Waubra farm using a computer-operated cutter to shape fins from the composite.

"I'd tried caravan walls and boat walls, but all of that has a super loose weave fibreglass that doesn't really lend itself to surfboard fins, and so that led me towards wind turbines," Mr Hunt said.

There are questions around how Australia will manage decommissioned wind turbine blades. (ABC News: Charlotte Wilkes)

While 90 per cent of a wind turbine can be recycled, the 10 per cent that cannot is the blades, which is a problem wind farms across the country are racing to solve.

According to the Clean Energy Council, there are 31 Australian wind farms more than 15 years old, and by 2034, decommissioned wind farms are estimated to produce 15,000 tonnes of blade composite waste.

Mr Hunt is offering a potential blueprint for managing the thousands of tonnes of blade waste predicted to hit Australian shores in the next decade.

Time is right

Acciona's Waubra Wind Farm is in its 16th year of operation.

General manager of brand and marketing Caroline Pinter said that while blade recycling was not a pressing issue today, it would inevitably become one.

"Finding solutions for these complex composite materials is not easy, and especially because wind turbine blades are so long," she said.

"The blades at the Waubra Wind Farm are 40 metres long, and modern blades are 80 metres long, so that's a significant amount of material and a significant challenge to transport them."

Mr Hunt said what made these turbine blades so difficult to recycle was also what made the material so perfect for surfboard fins.

Banjo Hunt says it has traditionally been labour-intensive to make fins. (Supplied: Christopher Chan)

He has spent the past few months making fins from a 6m-long portion of a turbine blade.

He said that by reusing the material, it avoided the most expensive and labour-intensive parts of traditional fin manufacturing, as well as keeping his company's fin production in Australia.

"It's quite an abundant resource, and it's certainly a step in the right direction compared to sourcing my materials otherwise, where it's expensive and toxic and comes from places I can't really track down," Mr Hunt said.

Banjo Hunt's surfboard fins are made from 100 per cent turbine blades. (Supplied: Christopher Chan)

According to Acciona, the turbine blade Mr Hunt has used to create fins generated 14,773 megawatt-hours of clean energy, avoiding 19,000 tonnes of carbon dioxide emissions during its operational life.

Tried and tested

Darcy Crump put the surfboard fins to test at the 2026 Australian Boardriders Battle. (Supplied: Christopher Chan)

Professional surfer Darcy Crump put the turbine blade fins to the test at the Australian Boardriders Battle on the Gold Coast last month.

"As a surfer, we're kind of always looking for renewable things, and how we can recycle in [the] best places, and surfboard fins was a pretty big one," Mr Crump said.

"So, having these fins made out of wind turbine blades was pretty special, and it turned a lot of heads while we were up on the coast."

Mr Crump said the fins felt "a little stiffer" than other commercially made ones, but noted that everyone liked something different.

"And for me, they were on par with all the big-name brands out there for fins, so I was happy with how they performed and got to use them at a pretty high level [of competition]."

Darcy Crump says he will keep using the turbine fins for surfing more powerful waves. (Supplied: Christopher Chan)

Solutions beyond the sea

Andrew Bray is the national director of RE-Alliance, an independent not-for-profit organisation helping regional communities in the renewable transition.

He said turning blades into surfboard fins was just one of many possible solutions to a problem that will become increasingly common.

"[Blades] are made up of an epoxy resin and materials which make them really strong and durable during their life, but it also means that they're harder to break down at the end of their life," Mr Bray said.

The Waubra Wind Farm is in regional Victoria. (ABC News: Charlotte Wilkes)

"A lot of recycling and decommissioning is happening in places like Europe already, but it hasn't really started happening here in Australia.

"[Overseas], we're seeing wind turbine blades turned into a different range of things, such as bus shelters, skis, furniture, and playground equipment."

Mr Bray said newer blades were being designed to be more easily recycled, so it was just older blades that required thinking outside the box.

"We're going to need a few [ideas] to make sure that these older blades can be recycled," he said.

World.title: Carlos Alcaraz's French Open three-peat dreams ended by wrist injury
World.content:
Carlos Alcaraz's hopes of a French Open three-peat have been ended after the world number two revealed a wrist injury has ruled him out of Roland Garros next month.

The seven-time grand slam champion picked up ​the injury in the first round ‌of the Barcelona Open earlier this month before withdrawing from the tournament.

Scans showed the issue was more serious than initially thought, after which the 22-year-old also withdrew from the Madrid Open.

The Spaniard said he would also ‌skip the Masters tournament in Rome.

"After the results of the tests carried out today, we have ⁠decided that the most prudent thing to do is to be cautious ‌and not participate in Rome or Roland ​Garros as we wait to ‌evaluate the progress so we can decide when to return to the court," Alcaraz said on social media.

Loading Instagram content

"This is a difficult time for me, but I am sure we will come out of it stronger."

Having won the Australian Open earlier this year, Alcaraz was gunning for his third straight Roland Garros ​crown ‌after also winning the title in 2024.

He will now skip the entire clay court swing, with an eye on Wimbledon in June.

The last time Alcaraz missed a major was the 2023 Australian ⁠Open due to a leg injury.

A clay court master, ‌Alcaraz won titles at Monte ‌Carlo, Rome and Roland Garros last year and also finished runner-up in Barcelona.

He beat current world number ‌one Jannik Sinner in last year's marathon final at Roland Garros, saving three championship points and coming back from two sets down to win after five hours and 29 minutes.

Jannik Sinner has urged Alcaraz not to rush back and risk further injury. (AP: Aurelien Morissard)

Alcaraz's withdrawal ‌paves the ​way for Sinner to potentially ⁠complete a career slam — the Italian has won the Australian Open twice, Wimbledon last year and the US Open in 2024 — but he said he simply hoped to see the Spaniard back on court soon.

"I don't know. I think this [his chances of winning] is not what we should talk about," Sinner said.

"I think most important is to say that, first of all tennis needs Carlos — tennis is in a much better spirit when he's around. And also for me personally it's nice when he's around, it makes me look also in the draw and single matches in a different way."

The nature of the injury is somewhat concerning considering the careers that have been curtailed or ended by wrist complaints.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

2009 US Open winner Juan Martin del Potro battled wrist issues for much of his career, Dominic Thiem started struggling with his wrist a year after his breakthrough US Open title in 2020 and retired in 2024, while Australian Nick Kyrgios has also endured difficulties.

"I do believe he's [Alcaraz] going to come back stronger than before. But injury is always tough, especially wrist," Sinner said.

"There are certain areas of our body which are very sensitive, and the wrist we saw with those other players in the past that they can complicate our lives … so, I hope he's gonna come back and he will not have any further injuries.

"But I also believe that it's good that he and his team takes the time, because if you come back too early then maybe you have bigger problem afterwards, and we all want that he's competitive from when he's gonna come back."

The main draw at the French Open gets underway on May 24, with the rest of the field aiming to become the first men's major singles winner not named Alcaraz or Sinner since 2023.

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

Reuters/ABC

World.title: 'Carry the hope': Thousands gather for Anzac Day service in Canberra
World.content:
Tens of thousands have gathered before sunrise at the Australian War Memorial in Canberra for Anzac Day, commemorating the 111th anniversary of the Gallipoli landings.

The dawn service began with a didgeridoo performance by Wiradjuri man and Flight Lieutenant James Evans before the crowd participated in a hymn.

Up to 35,000 people attended the ceremony, according to the War Memorial, with wreaths laid by Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and the New Zealand High Commissioner, Andrew Needs.

Since the Anzacs fought alongside one another in Turkey during World War I, experiencing high casualties, April 25 has come to represent a bond between the two nations.

A crowd watches on at the dawn service in Canberra. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

'My bags are always packed'

The commemorative address was given by Flying Officer Kbora Ali of the Royal Australian Air Force, whose family fled Afghanistan when she was a child.

"In 2001, in the early hours of the morning, a tiny wooden boat in the Indian Ocean was on the verge of sinking," her speech began.

She said the boat was slammed down "onto the unforgiving water" and those on board, including children, "didn't have much time left".

"Water was quickly filling up the broken boat and there was no land in sight," she said.

"Among the people that our courageous Navy personnel saved from that sinking boat was my father, who risked his life to try and find us safety.

"I didn't see my father for many years — our family wasn't together much during my childhood."

Flying Officer Kbora Ali speaks at the Anzac Day dawn service in Canberra. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

She said when she was 18 years old and her family was "living comfortably in Australia", she left home and went on to join the military.

"Now I am the one who is never home, my bags are always packed," she said.

"This is the kind of sacrifice that men and women of the Australian Defence Force make every single day.

"They do this so that other families can be spared the suffering and separation that occurs when home is no longer a safe place to stay."

Anthony Albanese attended the Anzac Day dawn service alongside his wife Jodie Haydon. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

Now an aviator, Flying Officer Ali said she gets to "carry the hope and now the promise to give back to a place I now call home".

The long 'legacy' of the Anzacs

Flying Officer Ali spoke of the meaning of Anzac Day and the courage shown by those who were in Gallipoli in 1915.

"We acknowledge that we can only serve on this journey because of their legacy and sacrifices," she said.

A child in the crowd at the Canberra dawn service. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

She said that in times of war and conflict, "our guiding principle should always be as those of the Anzacs before us, to uphold the values we cherish as Australians".

World.title: The donkey marching for the memory of all animals that serve in war
World.content:
Among the sights and sounds of uniformed servicemen and women, veterans and officials marching down the main street of Mount Gambier this Anzac Day will be the hoof-beats of a small grey donkey.

For the first time, Penny the donkey — hailing from Dartmoor in Victoria — will appear in the south-east South Australian city's Anzac parade, wearing a striking rug featuring 230 hand-knitted purple poppies.

"This is going to be a very memorable and moving sight," said Liz Wheeler, a Limestone Coast Veterans Hub wellbeing advocate and a former member of the Royal Australian Army Medical Corps.

Ms Wheeler hopes Penny will draw attention to the serving animals of wartime and their stories, and spark discussions about their role.

Heather Harrington knitted and crocheted poppies for the blanket. (Supplied: Liz Wheeler)

The rug — a sea of purple, lilac and some red poppies — was the work of a network of volunteers from Mount Gambier, as well as Victoria and Tasmania.

"It was this beautiful collaborative effort, led by Heather Harrington, and Penny will be the most dignified and beautifully adorned donkey this Anzac Day," Ms Wheeler said.

In the lead-up to the official march, Penny arrived in Mount Gambier on Anzac Day eve and tried on the rug.

"Donkeys are renowned for their reliability and intelligence, so we're pretty lucky to have found her just across the border in Dartmoor — she's quiet on the lead and used to crowds, so we think she and her handler will do a wonderful job," Ms Wheeler said.

Penny lives in the Dartmoor district in Victoria. (Supplied: Sarah Treloars)

International friends

The Mount Gambier Anzac Day March will assemble at 10am at the Old Town Hall before marching up Commercial Street to the Vansittart Soldier Memorial.

But beyond the majesty of the Anzac parade in the South Australian regional city, news of Penny's parade had travelled to Cheshire, in England, through a mutual connection with the Australian War Animals Memorial Organisation.

Colin the donkey has "written" a letter to Penny ahead of her march in Mount Gambier's Anzac Day commemorations. (Supplied: Liz Wheeler)

Ms Wheeler said she was "surprised and excited" to get an email from Colin, a donkey that takes part in the Purple Poppies Tour of Military Museums in Cheshire.

"In turn, we plan to have Penny pen a reply for Colin, which will feature in an educational magazine for school children," she said.

The Australian War Animals Memorial Organisation has organised its own procession in Cheshire with a few of its donkeys on April 25.

Colin the donkey will take part in a Anzac Day ceremony in Cheshire, England. (Supplied: Sarah Booth)

There will be an Australian and a New Zealand flag, Anzac Day biscuits, and the donkeys will also wear purple poppy rugs.

"We will be thinking of Penny undertaking her important role in the Mount Gambier Anzac Day march and wearing her lovely rug," the organisation said.

Ms Wheeler said the project, funded by an Anzac Day Commemoration Fund grant, also had unique significance for her.

"During my own service, I was particularly struck by the example of Simpson and his donkey, which reminds us that heroism is not only found in battle, but in the quiet and steadfast commitment to helping others, one wounded soldier and one donkey-led journey at a time," she said.

The 'Simpson legacy'

John Simpson Kirkpatrick — known simply as Simpson to generations of Australians — remains one of the most enduring symbols of courage, compassion and mateship to emerge from the Gallipoli campaign.

The English-born 22-year-old enlisted with the Australian Imperial Force on August 25, 1914, and served in the 3rd Field Ambulance Australian Army Medical Corps.

At Anzac Cove, he worked as a stretcher bearer.

The story of Private John Simpson Kirkpatrick is one of the most famous Anzac legends. (Supplied: Australian War Memorial)

The perilous role he undertook with the aid of a small donkey he found saw them carry wounded soldiers from the front lines, often under sniper and shrapnel fire.

Simpson was killed by machine gun fire just 24 days after the landing, during one of his morning rescue trips.

He was buried on the beach at Hell Spit, but stories of his heroics spread in dispatches and his legend was born.

Liz Wheeler says the project has a personal significance to her after her service with the Royal Australian Army Medical Corps. (ABC South East SA: Liz Rymill)

Ms Wheeler said she wanted the stories of Simpson and his donkey, as well as animal service in wartime, to spark the imaginations of everyone, from school children to families, veterans and present-day servicemen and women.

"By having Penny march down Mount Gambier's Main Street this Anzac Day, it keeps the legacy and memory of Simpson and his donkey alive," she said.

" It'll be a very special part of an important event. "

Diverse Anzac stories told

Penny's work is not the only example of a growing awareness of animal stories from the front lines.

Penny the donkey will take part in Mount Gambier's Anzac Day parade. (Supplied: Sarah Treloars)

Nicole Townsend, a lecturer in history at UNSW in Canberra, said animals had always been involved in war stories.

"If we look at Anzacs in the First World War particularly, we can see there's over 16 million animals that actually served in that conflict alone," Dr Townsend said.

"[They] served as transport, messengers, protectors, mascots, pets, companions and all sorts of roles."

Dr Townsend said commemorations like the National Day for War Animals on February 24, as well as the Australian Animal Distinguished Service Award, had continued to highlight the work of animals.

"It's something that's really acknowledged and … tugs at the heartstrings for many people when you see animals in war," she said.

"There are a few people internationally and in Australia that are really starting to look more at the role of animals."

Nicole Townsend says more Anzac Day commemorations are recognising the role animals play in war. (Supplied: Nicole Townsend)

While Anzac Day and its stories are still deeply revered by Australians and New Zealanders today, Dr Townsend says personal connections have broadened its reach internationally.

"Despite the fact that the presence of memorials and dawn services around Anzac Day do mean people within quite small towns in the Western Front are reminded of Australian involvement … it's not something that's as well known across the board," she said.

"These kinds of interpersonal and person-to-person contacts — like the pen pal aspects of [Penny and Colin's story] — really help to provide that intrinsic connection for people who might not otherwise have that connection."

World.title: Beaconsfield mine rescue continues to defy belief two decades on
World.content:
Brant Webb is cracking jokes and taking photos with star-struck tourists from the mainland.

Standing only metres away is the yellow, steel gate from which he and Todd Russell emerged into the frigid Tasmanian morning air almost two decades ago, embracing their loved ones as the nation rejoiced in their rescue.

Brant Webb became a household name after his rescue in 2006. (ABC News: Morgan Timms)

"Time flies when you're having fun," said Mr Webb, 57, reflecting on the past 20 years.

Late on Anzac Day in 2006, a minor earthquake caused a rockslide that claimed the life of Beaconsfield goldmine worker Larry Knight and triggered a two-week search and rescue effort that will live long in Australian memory.

Tasmanian miners Todd Russell and Brant Webb emerged on May 9, 2006, after being trapped underground for 14 days. (Ian Waldie/Pool: AAP)

Mr Webb and Mr Russell became household names when news broke that they had been found alive, precariously trapped inside a cage deep beneath their shell-shocked community.

In the years since, there have been films, books, countless interviews — and an unlikely friendship with rock 'n' roll royalty.

Beaconsfield miner Larry Knight died in the rockfall. (Supplied: Knight family)

But despite his "low-level celebrity" status, Mr Webb has always tried to stay grounded.

He is now a proud grandfather who earns a living renovating houses, having found a way of processing the ordeal.

"The worst time is when your mind's racing and you can't sleep and you don't understand why … but I've got a fair handle on all that now," he said.

" It's pretty amazing … your brain actually tries to get rid of a lot of stuff that isn't good. "

He has not lost sight, though, of how lucky he is to be alive.

"When the seismic activity was all going, there were a couple of times when we thought … this is all going to fall in," Mr Webb said.

"The rescuers are just phenomenal … for them to keep us alive for two weeks is pretty good."

'It can all just fall in'

Twenty years ago to the day, Greg Crowden was at home in Beaconsfield when he received a desperate late-night knock on the door.

But no amount of mine rescue training could have fully prepared him for the next fortnight.

"Initially, we just got some remote boggers [loaders] in and started bogging as far as you could into the mine — to the telehandler — where we thought we'd find them," he said.

Greg Crowden has remained friends with Brant Webb. (ABC News: Mackenzie Heard)

Mr Crowden was "quite shocked" when they found two of his colleagues still alive, but "devastated" by the discovery of Mr Knight's body.

He said the complexity of extracting the trapped pair could not be overstated.

"Imagine that a heap of rocks are just bound up on top of a basket, and if you pull a keystone out, it can all just fall in," he said.

"Every time we fired to get to them, it was rattling all the rocks and that sort of thing … they were scared themselves in there."

Greg Crowden embraced Brant Webb soon after he walked free from the mine in May 2006. (Supplied: Greg Crowden)

Mr Crowden was among the first people to communicate with his entombed colleagues after contact was made, passing on messages to Mr Webb — a close friend — from his wife, Rachel.

"It made my hair stand on end," he said.

" Just to hear their voices, and having a chat ... was just amazing. "

Mr Crowden said the rescue operation should be remembered as "a big team effort" with help coming from across the state and country.

"Everybody put their heads together to resolve a situation that was never done before," he said.

'Shocked' town bands together

A short and picturesque drive along the Tamar River from Launceston, Beaconsfield's population in 2006 was about 1,200.

The goldmine was its economic backbone.

As West Tamar mayor at the time, Barry Easther was never a morning person but for an unforgettable two-week period, he had little choice.

Barry Easther says he is proud of how the Beaconsfield community responded to the event. (ABC News: Morgan Timms)

A large part of Mr Easther's role was dealing with the community's unprecedented media attention.

Some national news crews were already descending on Tasmania for the 10th anniversary of the country's deadliest mass shooting at Port Arthur.

"The number of media outlets that were represented here in Beaconsfield was just absolutely amazing," he said.

" And I spent quite a deal of time speaking with them, starting very early in the morning. "

In 2006, then West Tamar mayor Barry Easther was regularly updating the media pack. (Supplied)

Mr Easther remembered the palpable mix of shock, anxiety and relief among locals, who banded together to support the rescue effort through meals, beds, prayers and any other means necessary.

When the moment finally arrived, before dawn on May 9 — "Freedom Day", in the words of Brant Webb — Mr Easther was speechless.

"They walked out with their arms in the air … and it was just something I couldn't believe had happened," he said.

"It was remarkable."

Bill Shorten says his role as AWU secretary was largely to ensure rank-and-file miners were not blamed for the incident. (AAP: Dale Cumming)

In April 2006, Bill Shorten was a 38-year-old national secretary of the Australian Workers' Union.

He was overseas when news spread of the rockfall. He still describes the subsequent fortnight in Tasmania's north as among the "most massive events" of his life.

"You couldn't walk past a tree without a cameraman falling out of the branches," said Mr Shorten, now vice-chancellor of the University of Canberra.

He said his role was to be "an umbrella to deflect the blame" from rank-and-file miners.

Bill Shorten, now vice-chancellor of the University of Canberra, says the Beaconsfield mine rescue was a remarkable event in Australian history. (ABC News: Mark Moore)

The former Labor leader said Mr Russell and Mr Webb had "kept their end of the bargain" in the two decades since they walked out of the mine.

"They have repaid their families who believed in them," Mr Shorten said.

"They've repaid their workmates, they've repaid Australians who were cheering them on.

" The reason why they survived looks them in the mirror every day. "

Museum honours mine's past

In their own ways, both men have remained involved in the Beaconsfield community.

Mr Russell recently retired from the volunteer fire brigade after more than 30 years of service.

Brant Webb says the Beaconsfield community has supported him and his family over the past two decades. (ABC News: Morgan Timms)

Stream I Was Actually There on ABC iview This bold six-part documentary explores defining moments of our recent history through the eyes, ears and voices of those who witnessed them firsthand.

Mr Webb still lives at Beauty Point — just down the road from the goldmine which ceased operations in 2012 and is now a popular museum.

Tourists have replaced the hard hats and hi-vis of yesteryear.

"Putting us back on the map, mate," laughs Mr Webb.

He is "a regular" at the museum, mainly due to the requests for tours he receives from visiting family and friends.

His grandfatherly role is one he takes seriously.

"I'm just happy if I can see my grandkids and my kids, and have part of their life," he said.

The Beaconsfield mine stopped operation in 2012 and is now a popular museum. (ABC News)

His smile vanishes when discussing the death of his friend Larry Knight, which he described as a "catastrophe" that should never have happened.

"We cannot thank our rescuers enough," Mr Webb said.

" I've got to take my hat off to them again … because without them, I wouldn't be sitting here talking to you. "

Listen to the extended conversation with Todd Russell on the I Was Actually There podcast or stream the entire series of I Was Actually There on ABC iview.

World.title: Inmates accused of sexual assault in prison continued to share cells, report finds
World.content:
Prisoners accused of sexually assaulting their cellmates at a Brisbane jail continued to share cells with other inmates on three separate occasions, a scathing report has revealed.

Brisbane Correctional Centre at Wacol stipulates an alleged perpetrator of sexual assault must be placed in solo accommodation.

The Queensland Ombudsman visited the jail in December 2024, reviewing 23 reported incidents of sexual assaults.

"Concerningly, we found that three prisoners had continued to share a cell at the centre while under investigation for sexual assault allegations against another prisoner," it noted.

In one incident, the case notes for a prisoner under investigation for the assault of his cellmate recorded there were "no issues or concerns about him sharing a cell".

He was later charged with the rape of his former cellmate, and a further 17 case notes and two audits by a supervisor "failed to identify any issues" with him sharing a cell.

The ombudsman found prisoner sexual assaults had gradually increased and were likely under-reported.

Brisbane Correctional Centre stipulates an alleged perpetrator of sexual assault must be placed in solo accommodation. (ABC News: Andree Withey)

Queensland Corrective Services (QCS) said work was underway to improve risk assessments around cell sharing.

"CS (Corrective Services) has a zero-tolerance approach to prisoner sexual assault and is committed to ensuring the safety and wellbeing of prisoners in its facilities."

Night shift staff 'eating and watching television'

The ombudsman found issues in checks on prisoners by night shift staff, with an intercom button in each cell used when an inmate needs assistance.

However, inmates told the ombudsman they often didn't press the intercoms, with assaults usually only found the following morning.

In one incident, a group threatened to rape a new prisoner, while his cellmate told him he would tie him up.

"He did not sleep that night and decided it would be better to end his life than be raped and bashed," the report said.

"At 5.52am, the control room called an emergency code after the prisoner's cellmate pressed his intercom button after waking up and seeing that the prisoner had cut his neck and there was blood all over his pillow and sheets."

The prisoner later told staff his cellmate had warned him pressing the intercom button would be "bailing".

The ombudsman report found issues in checks on prisoners by night shift staff at Brisbane Correctional Centre. (AAP: Jono Searle)

The report noted in one visit, most of the night shift staff were in the officers' mess hall "eating and watching television".

QCS said it would continue to review its night shift practices.

Overcrowding and 'double-ups'

Staff told the ombudsman some of the biggest challenges facing the centre were overcrowding and cell sharing, referred to as 'double-ups'.

In June, 2024 the jail's capacity was at 168 per cent.

"Concerningly, at the time of the onsite inspection, we were told that the centre was preparing for the possibility of 'triple-ups' or placing three prisoners to a cell, although these plans have not been finalised."

Following the ombudsman's visit, QCS noted new and expanded correctional centres would alleviate the overcrowding pressures.

The report noted concerns raised by prisoners about cell sharing fell on deaf ears. (AAP: Jono Searle)

The report reviewed cell-sharing risk assessments for 32 prisoners in late 2024.

"We found that there were no cell-sharing risk assessments for several prisoners, and for most prisoners, case notes were generic and appeared to have been copied from a template.

" For example, we reviewed one case note that contained the words 'insert specific factors'. "

Concerns raised by prisoners about cell sharing fell on deaf ears, as evidenced by "inappropriate signage".

In a statement, Corrective Services Minister Laura Gerber said the findings were "very concerning", and noted the government had fast-tracked the Lockyer Valley prison to boost capacity across the system.

A QCS spokesperson said the "majority of the recommendations have been actioned or are in progress".

World.title: Loud boos mar Anzac Day dawn service in Martin Place
World.content:
Updated NationalNSWAnzac Day Loud boos mar Anzac Day dawn service in Martin Place Patrick Begley and Jack Gramenz Updated April 25, 2026 — 7:43am ,first published 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Save this article for later Add articles to your saved list and come back to them anytime. Got it Share A A A

Two hours before the sun rose, they stood gathered in uniforms, blazers and hoodies to remember the fallen. Thousands of people attended the ANZAC Day dawn service at the Martin Place Cenotaph in Sydney, a camera drone winking above them, as wreathes were laid, hymns sung and tears shed. Loading “It’s much bigger than I thought,” said John Murray, 89, a Vietnam veteran who made the trip from Brisbane to see what he believed was the biggest dawn service in Australia. The son of a Rat of Tobruk, Murray wore a blue RAAF cap and a row of medals pinned to his coat, including a British Empire Medal for his services in medical evacuation. “They do it very well here,” he said of the ceremony. The minute of silence was solemn, unbroken. But earlier, a number of crowd members booed loudly and repeatedly during an Acknowledgment of Country by Uncle Ray Minniecon.



Minniecon, whose grandfather served with the Light Horse Brigade, continued despite the interruption and was applauded when he finished. Vietnam Veteran, 89-year-old John Murray at the ANZAC day dawn service in Martin Place, Sydney. Louise Kennerley Uncle Ray Minniecon whose Acknowledgment of Country was interrupted by loud booing. Louise Kennerley “We have experienced this type of racism for over 200 years,” he told media after the service. “One of the questions that we have in our minds is: What crime did we commit to attract this kind of racism?” NSW Police in a statement said officers responded to an alleged act of nuisance and arrested a 24-year-old man. Last year, a Welcome to Country during a dawn service in Melbourne was marred by boos by members of the neo-Nazi National Socialist Network.



On Saturday morning, the organiser for the anti-immigration March for Australia movement, Bec Freedom, posted on Telegram “Sydney boo’d”, followed by a salute emoji. March for Australia is closely linked to the National Socialist Network, which claims to have disbanded to avoid being proscribed as a hate group. Dawn service at Martin Place, Sydney. Louise Kennerley The service in Martin Place, Sydney, began at 4.20am. Louise Kennerley Crowds at the dawn service in Martin Place. Louise Kennerley



Emile Tauati, a warrant officer in the navy, said everyone was entitled to their opinion but “I do believe there’s a time and a place”. Tauati woke at 2am to attend the “very moving” service, his first in his hometown of Sydney after 16 years of military service. In previous years he was away, on base or at sea. Premier Chris Minns read the poem Salute by Sydney Elliott Napier, an annual tradition at the service. Other notable attendees included opposition leader Kellie Sloane, federal Social Services Minister Tanya Plibersek, Governor Margaret Beazley and acting head of the RSL, Brigadier Vincent Williams (retired). Stacey Nicholson with son two-year old son Bodhi woke early to attend the service at Martin Place. Louise Kennerley Paul Simpfendorfer, a warrant officer in the army who most recently deployed to South Sudan, said he was up before dawn to “remember people I’ve served with.” Some had lost their lives in operations, others in training. “For me, it’s paying respect to my forbears,” Simpfendorfer said.



Nicholson, whose uncle served in the military, attended her first service with her partner and two-year-old son Bodhi, who sucked on a pacifier while toying with a commemorative sprig of rosemary. “I think it’s always important to honour our history,” Nicholson said. “We are very, very lucky in the life we have. Thousands of people are expected to pay tribute to Australia’s veteran community at Anzac Day ceremonies and events across NSW and around Australia this long weekend. Projections on the Australian War Memorial in Canberra for the Anzac Day Dawn Service. Alex Ellinghausen Crowds gather for the Anzac Day Dawn Service at the Australian War Memorial in Canberra. Alex Ellinghausen



Where to commemorate Anzac Day in Sydney? The major official commemorations are taking place at the Martin Place Cenotaph and near the Anzac Memorial in Hyde Park. NSW will have a public holiday on Monday, April 27, as April 25 falls on a weekend this year. The Monday public holiday is part of a two-year trial that will also capture Anzac Day falling on a Sunday in 2027. The Anzac Day march in 2025. Sam Mooy The dawn service is followed by a march along Elizabeth Street at 9am, before a commemoration service at the Pool of Remembrance, near the Anzac Memorial in Hyde Park at 12.30pm.



A sunset service will take place at the Martin Place Cenotaph at 5pm. Former governor-general Peter Cosgrove in last year’s Anzac Day march. Sam Mooy Other community events are being held around the state by RSL sub-branches. In Parramatta, a march gathered at the town hall at 4am, proceeding to Prince Alfred Square before a dawn service at 4.30am. In Penrith, the dawn service assembled outside the Penrith RSL club before a silent march to Memory Park. The RSL club will be providing a breakfast following the service.



A Newcastle dawn service commenced at 5am at Camp Shortland on Nobbys Beach, before a march from Perkins Street to Civic Park at 9.15am and a commemoration service at Civic Park Cenotaph at 10am, featuring an RAAF flyover. A Wollongong dawn service, also at 5am, was held at the MacCabe Park Cenotaph on Church Street, followed by a march on Crown Street at 10am. How to get around the city on Anzac Day Participants parade down Elizabeth Street in the 2025 Anzac Day March. Louise Kennerley Major road closures are in place on Anzac Day and public transport is encouraged. Travel is free for veterans, currently serving ADF personnel, and their families. Eligibility applies for people in uniform, wearing their medals or with proof of military service.



Additional services will run to Martin Place, however light rail services will not run between Town Hall and Circular Quay until 6.15am, pausing again between 12.30pm and 1.30pm. Buses through the city may take different routes and stops. Related Article Perspective

Anzac Day ‘He died at the moment the war ended’: The young Australian who helped the Czech partisans What’s open and closed on Anzac Day? Anzac Day is a restricted trading day. Major retailers, including supermarkets and department stores, will be closed all day. Small shops, chemists, newsagencies, service stations, cafes, takeaway food outlets and licensed venues can open. The public holiday on Monday is not a restricted trading day. Where can I play two-up?



Two-up at the Clock Hotel, Surry Hills, in 2025. Sam Mooy Chances are if a pub is open on Anzac Day you’ll be able to play two-up there. It’s one of the three days of the year the game, played by World War One Diggers, is allowed. Venues don’t need a permit but have to ensure the game is played in its traditional format. World.title: 5 costs that catch landlords out – and how to minimise them
World.content:
Sponsored MoneyInvestingTerri Scheer Landlord Insurance 5 costs that catch landlords out – and how to minimise them Sponsored by Terri Scheer Landlord Insurance Simon Webster April 25, 2026 — 6:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Save this article for later Add articles to your saved list and come back to them anytime. Got it Share A A A

Being a landlord sounds easy: buy a property, rent it out to help pay off your mortgage, and hope it grows in value. But it’s not quite that simple. With costs rising, many landlords are doing it tough. “Landlords have been under immense financial pressure, despite the increase in rents,” says Cate Bakos, chair of Property Investment Professionals of Australia (PIPA), a professional body that supports and advocates for ethical property investment standards. “Interest rate hikes have hurt landlords, alongside higher costs for compliance and minimum standards. In some states, such as Victoria, heightened land tax obligations have been challenging, too.” Model the costs of an investment property before buying. iStock Many landlords have seen operational costs increase significantly, Bakos says. In PIPA’s 2025 Annual Investor Sentiment Survey, 60 per cent of landlord respondents reported cost increases of between 11 and 41 per cent over the year to August 2025



That doesn’t necessarily mean property investment is unsuitable. But it does mean that prospective landlords should go in with their eyes wide open. “It is essential that landlords model all costs, including new taxes,” Bakos says. “Understanding the ‘out of pocket’ expenses, including taxes, insurances, surprise maintenance costs, as well as compliance costs, can make the difference between holding and folding.” Here are five costs that can take first-time landlords by surprise, along with practical ways to plan for them and minimise the impact. 1. Compliance costs In some states, checks covering items such as smoke alarms and gas and electrical systems are mandatory before a property can be rented out. “Costs can range from $400 upwards,” Bakos says. “The sting in the tail occurs when bigger issues arise.”



What you can do about it: “We always recommend a thorough building inspection to flag potential issues,” Bakos says. You might also try to arrange access to the property prior to settlement, to get your compliance reports done early, and avoid delays getting tenants in place. 2. Rent defaults Tenants’ circumstances can change for reasons outside their control. They might lose their job, separate or become unwell. If rent isn’t paid, it can create financial stress for a landlord. “It’s not an option for a landlord to ask their bank for a pause on repayments due to a tenant’s non-payment,” Bakos says. What you can do about it: Landlord insurance may provide cover for certain loss-of-rent scenarios, Bakos says. Depending on the policy, landlord insurance can cover a range of loss-of-rent situations that may not be included in standard home and contents policies.



3. Essential services breaking down “We all know it,” Bakos says. “The hot water service decides to die. The oven door breaks. The heater packs up. These are essential items, and tenants have a right to have them fixed immediately.” What you can do about it: Regular maintenance may reduce the likelihood of some breakdowns, though sometimes things will just stop working. “Landlords should provision a suitable float to see to these items when they arise,” Bakos says. “A responsive landlord equates to a happy tenant-landlord relationship.” 4. Tenant damage Even with careful tenant selection, there is still a risk of accidental or unexpected damage to a property. Items can break, appliances can fail, and repairs can be more costly than anticipated.



“We all hope to avoid this one, but even the most seasoned investors will talk about this risk,” Bakos says. Tenant damage – whether that be malicious, deliberate (but not malicious) or accidental – is surprisingly common; landlord insurance specialist Terri Scheer says it is the most common claim category (followed by loss of rent). What you can do about it: Landlord insurance may help with some damage-related costs, Bakos says. Some landlords also use screening processes to help manage risk. 5. Managing your own property Self-managing a property, rather than hiring a property manager who may charge around 5 to 10 per cent of rent each month, may seem like a cost saving. However, a property manager may assist with tenant applications, day-to-day communication, and staying on top of maintenance and legal obligations. They can also be helpful if disputes arise, Bakos says. What you can do about it: Engaging a property manager can reduce some of the workload and risks associated with self-management, Bakos says. “Those who DIY it risk selecting a troublesome tenant and falling over if issues make it to the tribunal.”



Terri Scheer is Australia’s leading landlord insurance specialist. For more information, visit www.terrisheer.com.au. This article is general information only and does not take into account your objectives, financial situation or needs. Consider whether it is appropriate for you and seek independent advice before making any decisions. Insurance is issued by AAI Limited ABN 48 005 297 807, trading as Terri Scheer. Before buying insurance, read the Product Disclosure Statement (PDS) and Target Market Determination (TMD) available at www.terrisheer.com.au.

World.title: Loud boos mar Anzac Day dawn service in Martin Place
World.content:
Updated NationalNSWAnzac Day Loud boos mar Anzac Day dawn service in Martin Place Patrick Begley and Jack Gramenz Updated April 25, 2026 — 7:43am ,first published 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Save this article for later Add articles to your saved list and come back to them anytime. Got it Share A A A

Two hours before the sun rose, they stood gathered in uniforms, blazers and hoodies to remember the fallen. Thousands of people attended the ANZAC Day dawn service at the Martin Place Cenotaph in Sydney, a camera drone winking above them, as wreathes were laid, hymns sung and tears shed. Loading “It’s much bigger than I thought,” said John Murray, 89, a Vietnam veteran who made the trip from Brisbane to see what he believed was the biggest dawn service in Australia. The son of a Rat of Tobruk, Murray wore a blue RAAF cap and a row of medals pinned to his coat, including a British Empire Medal for his services in medical evacuation. “They do it very well here,” he said of the ceremony. The minute of silence was solemn, unbroken. But earlier, a number of crowd members booed loudly and repeatedly during an Acknowledgment of Country by Uncle Ray Minniecon.



Minniecon, whose grandfather served with the Light Horse Brigade, continued despite the interruption and was applauded when he finished. Vietnam Veteran, 89-year-old John Murray at the ANZAC day dawn service in Martin Place, Sydney. Louise Kennerley Uncle Ray Minniecon whose Acknowledgment of Country was interrupted by loud booing. Louise Kennerley “We have experienced this type of racism for over 200 years,” he told media after the service. “One of the questions that we have in our minds is: What crime did we commit to attract this kind of racism?” NSW Police in a statement said officers responded to an alleged act of nuisance and arrested a 24-year-old man. Last year, a Welcome to Country during a dawn service in Melbourne was marred by boos by members of the neo-Nazi National Socialist Network.



On Saturday morning, the organiser for the anti-immigration March for Australia movement, Bec Freedom, posted on Telegram “Sydney boo’d”, followed by a salute emoji. March for Australia is closely linked to the National Socialist Network, which claims to have disbanded to avoid being proscribed as a hate group. Dawn service at Martin Place, Sydney. Louise Kennerley The service in Martin Place, Sydney, began at 4.20am. Louise Kennerley Crowds at the dawn service in Martin Place. Louise Kennerley



Emile Tauati, a warrant officer in the navy, said everyone was entitled to their opinion but “I do believe there’s a time and a place”. Tauati woke at 2am to attend the “very moving” service, his first in his hometown of Sydney after 16 years of military service. In previous years he was away, on base or at sea. Premier Chris Minns read the poem Salute by Sydney Elliott Napier, an annual tradition at the service. Other notable attendees included opposition leader Kellie Sloane, federal Social Services Minister Tanya Plibersek, Governor Margaret Beazley and acting head of the RSL, Brigadier Vincent Williams (retired). Stacey Nicholson with son two-year old son Bodhi woke early to attend the service at Martin Place. Louise Kennerley Paul Simpfendorfer, a warrant officer in the army who most recently deployed to South Sudan, said he was up before dawn to “remember people I’ve served with.” Some had lost their lives in operations, others in training. “For me, it’s paying respect to my forbears,” Simpfendorfer said.



Nicholson, whose uncle served in the military, attended her first service with her partner and two-year-old son Bodhi, who sucked on a pacifier while toying with a commemorative sprig of rosemary. “I think it’s always important to honour our history,” Nicholson said. “We are very, very lucky in the life we have. Thousands of people are expected to pay tribute to Australia’s veteran community at Anzac Day ceremonies and events across NSW and around Australia this long weekend. Projections on the Australian War Memorial in Canberra for the Anzac Day Dawn Service. Alex Ellinghausen Crowds gather for the Anzac Day Dawn Service at the Australian War Memorial in Canberra. Alex Ellinghausen



Where to commemorate Anzac Day in Sydney? The major official commemorations are taking place at the Martin Place Cenotaph and near the Anzac Memorial in Hyde Park. NSW will have a public holiday on Monday, April 27, as April 25 falls on a weekend this year. The Monday public holiday is part of a two-year trial that will also capture Anzac Day falling on a Sunday in 2027. The Anzac Day march in 2025. Sam Mooy The dawn service is followed by a march along Elizabeth Street at 9am, before a commemoration service at the Pool of Remembrance, near the Anzac Memorial in Hyde Park at 12.30pm.



A sunset service will take place at the Martin Place Cenotaph at 5pm. Former governor-general Peter Cosgrove in last year’s Anzac Day march. Sam Mooy Other community events are being held around the state by RSL sub-branches. In Parramatta, a march gathered at the town hall at 4am, proceeding to Prince Alfred Square before a dawn service at 4.30am. In Penrith, the dawn service assembled outside the Penrith RSL club before a silent march to Memory Park. The RSL club will be providing a breakfast following the service.



A Newcastle dawn service commenced at 5am at Camp Shortland on Nobbys Beach, before a march from Perkins Street to Civic Park at 9.15am and a commemoration service at Civic Park Cenotaph at 10am, featuring an RAAF flyover. A Wollongong dawn service, also at 5am, was held at the MacCabe Park Cenotaph on Church Street, followed by a march on Crown Street at 10am. How to get around the city on Anzac Day Participants parade down Elizabeth Street in the 2025 Anzac Day March. Louise Kennerley Major road closures are in place on Anzac Day and public transport is encouraged. Travel is free for veterans, currently serving ADF personnel, and their families. Eligibility applies for people in uniform, wearing their medals or with proof of military service.



Additional services will run to Martin Place, however light rail services will not run between Town Hall and Circular Quay until 6.15am, pausing again between 12.30pm and 1.30pm. Buses through the city may take different routes and stops. Related Article Perspective

Anzac Day ‘He died at the moment the war ended’: The young Australian who helped the Czech partisans What’s open and closed on Anzac Day? Anzac Day is a restricted trading day. Major retailers, including supermarkets and department stores, will be closed all day. Small shops, chemists, newsagencies, service stations, cafes, takeaway food outlets and licensed venues can open. The public holiday on Monday is not a restricted trading day. Where can I play two-up?



Two-up at the Clock Hotel, Surry Hills, in 2025. Sam Mooy Chances are if a pub is open on Anzac Day you’ll be able to play two-up there. It’s one of the three days of the year the game, played by World War One Diggers, is allowed. Venues don’t need a permit but have to ensure the game is played in its traditional format. Liquor & Gaming NSW inspectors will be checking. Related Article Anzac Day Meet Fred, the Sydney Harbour Bridge-loving, Trump-hating 100-year-old veteran Are double demerits in effect? Yes. Double demerits are already in force and will continue throughout the weekend, including Monday. Random breath testing and mobile drug testing will also be conducted across the state. You can expect an increased police presence on major highways and regional routes due to expected increases in traffic over the long weekend. World.title: ‘The roads are dead’: PM’s fuel warning doomed outback tourism
World.content:
Charleville Bush Caravan Park operator Matthew Bom sits near his site’s empty fire pit area. Each night, he would usually be surrounded by travellers sharing their stories, but not this year.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

People are just cancelling, caravan park operator Kathryn Doyle says. “Left, right and centre. It’s just so sad out here.” It is 11am when Doyle answers the phone at Longreach Caravan Park, 13 hours north-west of Brisbane, in the heart of outback Queensland. Doyle is upbeat but steeling herself when she picks up the line – already that morning, three people had called to cancel their bookings. The global fuel crisis is hitting this year’s peak tourism season in outback Queensland even before it gets under way. At least 30 bookings have been cancelled at Longreach Caravan Park since the Big Red Bash was scrapped, according to Kathryn Doyle. The scenario is in stark contrast to the post-COVID boom, when international travel ground to a halt and Australians answered a rallying cry to support tourism operators in their own backyard. Australians in their droves jumped in caravans and headed to the outback. An industry that had its biggest moment in one crisis has been brought to its knees in the next. Australia’s cooler months, from April to the end of September, are peak season for outback tourism operators.



Southerners fleeing the colder capitals, and Brisbaneites alike, travel north in pursuit of adventure and temperatures in the mid-20s. Easter typically kicks things off. But not this year. On April 1, two days before Good Friday, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese addressed the nation, encouraging people to conserve fuel. Matthew Bom, 66, spent the summer planting 380 trees and hauling tonnes of bush rock to re-landscape 25 garden beds in preparation for this year’s peak outback tourism period. “But I’ve got no one here,” the Charleville Bush Caravan Park manager says. Bom fears the strain of the fuel crisis will wipe out more outback businesses than the pandemic had. “It’s going to be a catastrophe out here,” he says.



“There are stores – not just here in Charleville, but all throughout west out here, all the way up to Longreach and Winton and all that – that are stocked up ready for the peak season because this is the time when we get busy. “Everyone’s invested a lot of money. And now we’ve got nothing. The roads are dead.” Bom near the garden beds he spent hours replanting over summer in preparation for the peak travel season. Matthew Bom The first sign of trouble came with the record-breaking rain in February and March – parts of outback Queensland copped a year’s worth of rain in two days – which forced the cancellation of July’s Birdsville Big Red Bash. At least 30 bookings have been cancelled at Doyle’s Longreach Caravan Park since the Big Red Bash was scrapped, and she says occupancy is now the lowest it’s ever been. “Hardly anyone’s booking in,” Doyle says. “Guests are just saying, ‘We can’t come all the way out there when we don’t know what the fuel shortages are going to be like.’ So, unfortunately, there are more cancellations than there are bookings. Everyone’s suffering.”



Mixed messaging from federal and state governments urging Australians to keep their travel plans but also conserve fuel has been frustrating at a time when Queensland’s outback is uncharacteristically green and vibrant. “To paint a picture,” says Winton Shire Mayor Cathy White, “the landscape is absolutely a vision splendid after the recent flooding – the wildlife is incredible, and the wild flowers are blooming. The country’s never looked so beautiful. Charleville Bush Caravan Park would usually be full of travellers this time of year. This tourist season, it’s empty. Matthew Bom “But unfortunately, due to this fuel crisis, and the mixed messaging ... it’s putting doubt in people’s minds.” Every accommodation site this masthead spoke to said there was no shortage of fuel in their town, but no one to buy it. Winton, the birthplace of Qantas, is the home of the Australian Age of Dinosaurs Museum and the Waltzing Matilda Centre.



“I just want to get the message out there loud and clear … We’ve got fuel. You are not taking it from locals. We want you to come out and visit our beautiful part of the world,” White says. White was preparing for an emergency brainstorming meeting with Winton tourism operators this week to discuss ways to promote special accommodation and tour deals and entice people to “recharge, refuel and linger longer” in the outback. Kylie Rixon says outback tourism has a small and important peak season. Joanna Giemza-Meehan About six hours north-west, in Mount Isa – the city famous for Australia’s largest rodeo – Kylie Rixon has operated the Sunset Tourist Park for the past six years. She did not appreciate the prime minister’s message. “We’re only busy six months of the year and that one little comment ... from the prime minister telling people to be conservative ... it puts a knife in our hearts,” she says. “It’s really cruel. We rely on tourism as our backbone. It’s our bread and butter. It’s our livelihood. So to hear someone on such a big platform and with his authority to say ‘limit travel’ … that’s shithouse.”

World.title: Auckland liquor licences axed or suspended after selling booze to teen Silas Sims before fatal crash
World.content:
First published on

Photo: Open Justice

Teenager Silas Sims and his underage mates were sold alcohol at three different venues before he jumped into a car, drove drunk and crashed into a power pole.

The much-loved 16-year-old was pronounced dead at the scene. His blood contained more than three times the legal alcohol limit for adult drivers.

Last month, eight months on from the fatal crash, the two bars that sold him drinks on 19 July last year had their liquor licences suspended. The liquor shop that sold alcohol to Silas and his friend three times that day has had its licence cancelled.

In making those decisions, the Alcohol Regulatory and Licensing Authority said a "disturbing" if not "alarming" feature of the case was the "apparent ease" with which the young men were able to buy drinks, without any efforts to check their ages.

Silas' parents, who pushed for the venues to be prosecuted, have told NZME they are glad there have been repercussions.

While they did not want any businesses to be shut down, they were satisfied that the consequences were "part of deterrence".

"We did want it to be a big case in so much as a wake-up call," Silas' father, Benjamin Sims, said.

"Those sentences have been that."

Day-drinking in Matakana

On the day he died, Silas had made plans to meet up with two friends, whose names are suppressed, in Matakana, north of Auckland, to drink and smoke cannabis.

He first entered the Matakana Liquor Centre alone after 2pm and asked duty manager Tracey Brown where the Jägermeister was.

She showed him, and he bought a 700ml bottle of the 35 percent alcohol spirit. He was not asked for ID.

An hour and a half later, he and a friend arrived at popular music venue the Leigh Sawmill Cafe, in Leigh, 15 minutes' drive northeast of Matakana.

Silas ordered two beers from owner and duty manager Edward Guinness.

Silas was asked his age; he told Guinness he was 18 and was not asked to prove it.

He failed at buying a second round, however, and was told he had "had enough".

Then, the pair met up with a third friend and again entered the liquor store.

Silas bought a four-pack of rum and colas, while his friend bought an 18-pack.

They were served by two different staff members, including duty manager Johann Graas. Neither was asked for ID.

At 5.45pm, the pair went to the Matakana Village Pub, where they bought a rum and cola and a Guinness.

Silas' two friends tried to dissuade him from driving home and tried to take his keys.

But he persisted and, while driving along Leigh Road, on a left-hand bend, he crossed the centre line, left the road and crashed into a concrete power pole in a paddock.

He was pronounced dead after being removed from his car by paramedics.

An autopsy showed he had 193 micrograms of alcohol per 100 millilitres of blood. Drivers under 20 aren't allowed to have any alcohol in their system; the adult limit is 50mg.

Without fear

Photo: Open Justice

Silas' parents described their son as outgoing, charming and fearless.

"He could walk into a room and talk to anybody, from the day he could speak," his father said.

"He didn't have enough fear," his mother, Sarah Sims, added. "... and that's heartbreaking.

"It was just a lot of bad luck, and I so wish he was here."

She told NZME her son looked older than he was.

"He is the kid that would get served. He looked 20."

By the time he was served at the Matakana pub, he was "really, really rotten", she said.

CCTV footage showed him stumbling around the pub.

His mother became emotional as she said she wished someone at the venue, after taking her son's money, had also looked out for him.

Denying liability

The venues responded differently to the police applications to have their liquor licences suspended or cancelled.

The owners of the Leigh Sawmill Cafe and the Matakana Village Pub accepted the applications.

However, the Matakana Liquor Centre, owned by Micmat Ltd, denied liability.

Micmat owners John and Louise Walsh told the authority they had taken extensive steps to ensure alcohol was not sold to minors at their store.

There were multiple wall signs at the shop, even for the staff, and rigorous staff training and declarations to ensure that the law was followed.

Despite all these precautions, Silas and his friend were not asked for ID a total of three times in three hours, the authority found.

They were therefore found liable.

Photo: Open Justice

The duty managers

Duty manager Brown, who sold Silas the bottle of Jägermeister, had her manager's certificate suspended for two months.

The certificate of the store's second manager, Graas, had already lapsed, and he had left the industry, so the application against him was dismissed.

Leigh Sawmill owner Guinness admitted breaching the law and contributing to Silas' death.

He told the authority he was "embarrassed" and admitted he had "messed this one up".

His certificate was suspended for eight weeks.

Christopher King, duty manager of the Matakana pub at the time, gave evidence that, when Silas came into the bar, he was complaining of a splinter in his hand.

There was a brief moment, as King shone a torch on Silas' hand and got him tweezers, when they were in close proximity.

King told the hearing it never crossed his mind that Silas was a minor, as he appeared "broad-shouldered and confident".

On reflection, he accepted he may have been distracted, but Silas had none of the "red flags" of drunkenness, such as smelling of alcohol.

The authority found it "difficult to understand" how King had not found Silas to be drunk, considering the teen left the pub and was killed 20 minutes later.

King's certificate was suspended for 12 weeks.

Consequences

Leigh Sawmill's liquor licence was suspended for two weeks from 14-26 April, and the business has closed for that time.

The Matakana Village Pub, which now has a new owner, had its licence suspended for 21 days, from 29 April to 19 May.

Matakana Liquor Centre's licence was cancelled, and the company was given 21 days to close the business.

Its lawyer, Andrew Braggins, told NZME an appeal against the cancellation had been lodged.

A representative from Leigh Sawmill Cafe told NZME it felt the matter had been "dealt with" and did not wish to comment any further.

Deborah Body, who owned the Matakana pub at the time, said she deeply regretted the incident.

She had accepted all the applications the police made and co-operated "from the outset".

"We knew what we had done," she told NZME. "There was no question for us."

The liquor store owners declined to comment.

Police said they could not speak about the proceedings as Silas' death was still before the coroner's office.

They could not say whether any criminal charges would be laid in future for the same reason.

Actioning change

Meanwhile, Silas' parents say taking a more "positive" and active approach and effecting change has helped with their grief.

Benjamin Sims, a web developer, said he looked at his son's bank statements after he died and noticed that purchases at alcohol stores were classed as "restricted" by the bank, because Silas was underage.

He has gathered signatures for a petition that is currently before a parliamentary committee to require banks to restrict or block such payments.

"[Banks] make billions of dollars a year. [They] can afford to do this.

"It's not about alcohol; it's about all restricted goods."

- This story originally appeared in the New Zealand Herald.

World.title: Bay of Plenty highway closed, one seriously injured after crash
World.content:
Photo: RNZ / Nate McKinnon

Part of State Highway 36 in Ngongotahā, Bay of Plenty has been closed and a person left seriously injured after a crash on Saturday morning.
